title: Unit Pricing: How to Compare Prices Fairly
description: How to normalize prices across different sizes, periods and packages — unit price, price per ounce, per seat, per month — so discounts and subscriptions become genuinely comparable.
content:
Raw prices lie by omission. A $12 option and a $9 option are not comparable until you know what each contains; a $9.99 monthly plan and an $89 annual plan cannot be judged on their sticker prices. Unit pricing is the discipline of converting every price to a common denominator before comparing.

## The core move

Unit price = total price ÷ quantity of the thing you actually consume.

- **Retail packages.** $6.49 for 24oz versus $8.99 for 64oz: divide by ounces → $0.27/oz versus $0.14/oz. The larger pack is roughly half the price per ounce despite the higher sticker.
- **Subscriptions.** Divide by time or by seats. $9.99/month versus $89/year: the annual works out to $7.42/month — 26% cheaper per month.
- **Per-seat software.** A 5-seat plan at $50/month is $10/seat; a 3-seat plan at $36 is $12/seat. Compare per-seat, then check whether you actually need all five seats.

The denominator must be the quantity you value: ounces for consumables, months for time, seats for teams, uses for durables (more on that below).

## Where unit pricing gets subtle

**Waste and minimums.** The cheaper per-unit pack may exceed what you can use before it expires. Effective unit price = price ÷ units you will actually consume, not units bought.

**Tier differences.** When packages differ in quality tier (grass-fed versus conventional, pro versus base software), you are comparing different products. Normalize price only after deciding the tiers are interchangeable.

**Promotional pricing.** First-month discounts, annual-only sales and coupon codes distort the arithmetic. Recalculate with the price you will actually pay in month two, month six and month twelve.

**Hidden units.** Some products hide the quantity: "serving sizes" vary by brand, "pages per cartridge" assumes coverage that rarely holds. Where the published unit is unreliable, compare on a unit you can verify yourself.

## Annual vs monthly: annualize first

Subscriptions are the most common place people misjudge value. Convert everything to both monthly and annual equivalents:

1. Monthly plan: annual = monthly × 12.
2. Annual plan: monthly = annual ÷ 12.
3. Compare monthly-to-monthly and annual-to-annual.
4. Difference = (monthly−annual equivalents) ÷ average × 100 for a symmetric percentage gap.

Beyond cost, weigh lock-in: an annual plan paid upfront is cheaper but harder to exit. If you might cancel mid-year, the monthly plan's higher price is partly an option fee — sometimes worth paying deliberately.

## Cost per use: for things you buy to use

For durables — a pair of shoes, a camera, a tool — the fairest denominator is uses. A $120 jacket worn 100 times costs $1.20 per wear; a $40 jacket worn twice costs $20 per wear. Cost per use reframes cheap purchases as expensive ones and expensive purchases as cheap, provided you estimate uses honestly. The same math evaluates repair versus replacement: a $180 repair extending a device by two years against a $900 replacement is $75/month versus $37.50/month of fresh device life — though reliability risk belongs in the judgment too.

## Running the numbers

You can do all of this on paper, but the Unit Price, Monthly-vs-Annual and Cost-Per-Use calculators exist to make the arithmetic reliable: enter both prices and quantities, get the normalized figures, the percentage gap and the cheapest-per-unit verdict — with the formula shown so you can audit it. Use the result as the cost leg of your decision, then re-attach the non-cost differences (quality, lock-in, convenience) that the number deliberately ignored.
